drop.title: The Core That Springs From Nothing

title: The Core That
Springs From Nothing
slides.dek: A random graph's giant component grows in gently, the instant links average one per node. Peel the same graph a different way, deleting everyone with fewer than three neighbours, and the three-core stays flat at zero far past that point, then springs in all at once, born already holding a quarter of the graph.

slides.body: Ask not *what is connected to what* but *who is well-connected enough to stay*. Pick a number k and delete every node with fewer than k neighbours. But deleting a node lowers each neighbour's degree, so some of *them* now fall below k and must go too, and the deletions cascade. What survives is the *k-core*: a subgraph where every node still has at least k neighbours among the survivors. Named by Béla Bollobás in 1984, and unique, peel in any order you like and you land on the same core. The 2-core is the graph with every dangling tendril trimmed. The 3-core asks for something genuinely robust, and the way it *arrives* is the whole surprise.

Build a fresh graph for each average degree, peel it to its k-core, and plot the surviving fraction. The 2-core behaves like the giant component: it lifts off at one link each and rises smoothly, because it *is* the giant with its dead ends trimmed. Switch to k = 3 and the curve clings to *exactly zero*, out to an average degree near *3.35*, then jumps straight to more than a third of the graph in a single step. Grow the graph from 250 nodes to 12,000 and that jump tightens into a *vertical cliff*, a genuine discontinuity, the fingerprint of a first-order transition. The 4-core does the same, later and higher, near 5.15.

checked offline first, vs pittel-spencer-wormald (1996) and a direct peel: c_3 = 3.351 (born 26.8%), c_4 = 5.149 (43.8%), c_5 = 6.799 (53.9%); measured fraction tracks theory to ~0.001 above threshold

slides.big:
demand three links,
and the core is empty,
then it *jumps into being.*
slides.sub: Peel a graph yourself and watch the 3-core vanish or snap back across a tiny turn of the dial. Watch the double jump sharpen into a vertical cliff as the graph grows from 250 nodes to 12,000. Then read the one self-consistency curve behind it: at k = 2 it leaves the origin tangent to the line and the core grows in smoothly; at k = 3 and up it is flat at the origin and only catches the line far out, so the core is finite the instant it exists. There is no small core for it to be born into.
